findings.original: a host runs dozens of programs at once
findings.correction: a host can run many programs at once
findings.reason: Do not require a fixed program-count range.

findings.original: A DNS server uses one socket to talk to millions of clients
findings.correction: A DNS server can use one bound UDP socket for requests from many different client endpoints
findings.reason: One socket does not guarantee million-client capacity.

findings.original: and for live data it is worse than the loss itself
findings.correction: and independent deadline-sensitive updates can prefer skipping stale data to waiting for that gap
findings.reason: Tradeoff depends on application; not every live datum can be safely lost.

findings.original: A client talking to one destination is limited by its ephemeral port range
findings.correction: With one fixed source address and automatic allocation confined to a range, simultaneous connections to one destination are limited by that source-port pool
findings.reason: Multisource/manualbind cases differ; match scoped body.

findings.original: UDP has no sequence numbers, so it cannot reorder anything. Datagrams can arrive in any order.
findings.correction: Base UDP does not specify ordered delivery or receive-side resequencing. Applications can add their own sequence information and ordering policy.
findings.reason: Avoid inferring guarantees solely from header fields.

findings.original: A single loss is routine and is repaired by retransmission; it doesn't reset the connection.
findings.correction: One lost segment does not by itself instruct TCP to reset. Recovery is normally attempted; repeated failure can eventually reach an implementation or application timeout.
findings.reason: Loss recovery is not an unconditional success guarantee.

findings.original: SYN floods fill the half-open queue; SYN cookies encode the state in the ISN so nothing is stored until the client proves it saw the SYN+ACK.
findings.correction: SYN floods can exhaust establishment resources; SYN cookies avoid an ordinary per-attempt half-open entry while retaining shared state and consuming processing resources. Valid cookie acknowledgements are a return-path check, not cryptographic client identity.
findings.reason: Summary contradicted corrected body: sharedstate exists andfinitecookie notproofidentity.

findings.original: RST aborts immediately: refused connections, unknown connections, abortive closes and unread data on close.
findings.correction: An accepted valid RST normally aborts the connection; invalid resets may be ignored or challenged. Refused attempts, unknown connections and some close paths can generate resets.
findings.reason: Summary must respect validity/state-specific RST processing.

findings.original: [RFC 5961](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5961) makes stacks accept an RST only if its sequence number exactly matches the next expected byte.
findings.correction: For synchronized connections, [RFC 5961](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5961) specifies accepting an RST only when its sequence number exactly matches the next expected sequence-space position. Opening-state reset validation follows separate rules.
findings.reason: Do not universalize synchronized-state RST rule to SYN-SENT.

findings.original: Positive ordinary integer byte positions are required:
findings.correction: Nonnegative ordinary integer byte positions and positive interval lengths are required:
findings.reason: Match the executable validation, which permits position zero.

findings.original: but keeping flows on one path (per-flow ECMP hashing) is still the norm.
findings.correction: and per-flow ECMP hashing can reduce reordering caused by per-packet path changes.
findings.reason: Remove unsupported deployment-wide prevalence claim.

findings.original: **Reliability ends at the kernel.**
findings.correction: **Transport acknowledgement is not application acknowledgement.**
findings.reason: TCP endpoints may be implemented in user space; boundary is semantic not necessarilykernel.

findings.original: Fast retransmit resends after three duplicate ACKs, but fails for tail losses and small windows.
findings.correction: Classic fast retransmit uses three qualifying duplicate ACKs; without additional mechanisms, insufficient following data can leave tail losses or small flights waiting for the timer.
findings.reason: Scope summary to algorithm and sufficientevidence conditions.

findings.original: Because a single duplicate is often caused by packets arriving out of order, not by loss
findings.correction: A single duplicate ACK can result from packet reordering rather than loss
findings.reason: Avoid unverifiedfrequencyoftenclaim;possibility explainsheuristic.

findings.original: The whole point of fast retransmit is to beat the timer, which is usually much slower than a few RTTs.
findings.correction: Fast retransmit is intended to recover before RTO expiry when enough qualifying duplicate ACKs arrive; there is no universal ordering between an arbitrary few RTTs and the configured timer.
findings.reason: Remove unsupportedtimeralwaysslowerfewRTTscomparison.

findings.original:
1. Suppose segments A, B, C are sent and B is delayed slightly so the order becomes A, C, B.
2. After C the receiver sends a duplicate ACK (still waiting for B). When B arrives, the ACK jumps past C.
3. If the sender had resent B on the first duplicate, that retransmission would be wasted, and it would also have cut its sending rate for nothing.
4. In the simple example with one ACK per arrival, three duplicates provide stronger evidence of a hole; they do not universally prove three distinct later segments or actual loss. Modern RACK uses timing instead of a count for the same reason.
findings.correction:
1. Suppose segments A, B, C are sent and B is delayed slightly so the order becomes A, C, B.
2. After C the receiver sends a duplicate ACK (still waiting for B). When B arrives, the ACK jumps past C.
3. If the sender had resent B on the first duplicate, that retransmission would be wasted, and a congestion response could reduce its sending allowance unnecessarily.
4. In the simple example with one ACK per arrival, three duplicates provide stronger evidence of a hole; they do not universally prove three distinct later segments or actual loss. Modern RACK uses timing instead of a count for the same reason.
findings.reason: Congestionwindowchange isnot guaranteed measuredsendingratechange.

findings.original: If the sender just blasted bytes, the receiver's kernel buffer would fill and everything after that would be dropped, then retransmitted, then dropped again.
findings.correction: Without receiver flow control, sustained arrivals faster than the application drains them can exhaust finite receive buffering and cause drops. Retransmitting does not remove that bottleneck.
findings.reason: Scope overflow to sustained excess arrival and avoid a universal drop/retransmit cycle.

findings.original: As the application calls `recv()`, the buffer drains and the receiver advertises a bigger window. If the application stops reading, the window shrinks to zero and the sender must stop.
findings.correction: As the application calls `recv()`, the buffer drains and window-update policy can permit a larger advertised window. If the application stops reading while data continues to arrive, finite receive capacity can be exhausted: the receiver advertises zero and the sender must stop ordinary new-data transmission.
findings.reason: Window updates are policy-dependent; a stopped reader alone does not imply immediate zero window.

findings.original: every window update can move the right edge.
findings.correction: An accepted window update can change the right edge.
findings.reason: Invalid or stale advertisements need not update sender state.

findings.original: The window can only be as large as the receive buffer.
findings.correction: The advertised window must be supported by the receiver’s capacity and update policy; it is not a direct byte-for-byte reading of allocated socket memory.
findings.reason: Avoid equating sequence-space advertisement with memory allocation.

findings.original: was written for Telnet, where every keystroke became a 41-byte packet carrying 1 byte of data.
findings.correction: addresses, among other cases, interactive terminal traffic where a one-byte keystroke could occupy a 41-byte IPv4/TCP packet with minimal headers.
findings.reason: RFC 896 describes a possible interactive small-packet case, not a property of every Telnet keystroke.

findings.original: the sender keeps in-flight data within min(rwnd, cwnd).
findings.correction: ordinary new-data sending is constrained by both rwnd and cwnd; shrinkage, recovery and probes need additional rules.
findings.reason: Already-in-flight data need not instantly fall below a newly reduced window.

findings.original: Throughput is capped at window / RTT.
findings.correction: In the fixed-window steady-state model, throughput is capped at window / RTT.
findings.reason: Carry the model assumptions into the summary.

findings.original: A zero window stops the sender; the persist timer's probes stop a lost window update causing deadlock.
findings.correction: A zero window stops ordinary new-data transmission; successfully delivered persist probes and replies can recover from a lost window update.
findings.reason: Probes do not guarantee progress through persistent loss or endpoint failure.

findings.original: Nagle (sender) and delayed ACK (receiver) together stall write-write-read patterns by the delayed-ACK timeout.
findings.correction: Nagle (sender) and delayed ACK (receiver) can stall a split write-write-read exchange until the delayed-ACK timer expires.
findings.reason: Not every pair of writes produces the required packet/ACK timing.

findings.original:
1. The receiver advertises how many more bytes its buffer can hold.
2. The sender keeps in-flight data within `min(rwnd, cwnd)`.
3. rwnd protects the **receiver**; cwnd protects the **network**. Different problems, different windows.
findings.correction:
1. The receiver advertises an acceptable sequence range, reflecting buffering and update policy rather than exactly reporting free memory.
2. In the simplified ordinary new-data model, the remaining budget is `max(0, min(rwnd, cwnd) - flight)`.
3. rwnd provides receiver flow control; cwnd controls network congestion. Recovery, probes and window shrinkage require additional rules.
findings.reason: Align worked explanation with corrected sequence-space definition.

findings.original: The client would be limited by cwnd, but the server wouldn't advertise zero. Zero windows come from the receiver's buffer.
findings.correction: A small cwnd can coexist with a zero receive window, but it does not explain the independently observed blocked receiving thread and full receive queue.
findings.reason: Do not treat independently controlled windows as mutually exclusive.

findings.original: Bulk transfers send full segments, which Nagle doesn't hold.
findings.correction: Full-sized ready segments are not held by Nagle’s small-segment rule, although partial tails and incremental writes can be affected. The supplied captures establish the window-scaling problem in this scenario.
findings.reason: Bulk transfer does not guarantee all application writes produce full segments.

findings.original: A sender has MSS 1,460 bytes, cwnd = 40 segments, the receiver advertises rwnd = 256 KB (262,144 bytes), and 30,000 bytes are currently unacknowledged. How many more bytes may it send right now? Use the simplified new-data budget, with consistent ACK/window origins, no recovery/probe exceptions, and sufficient queued data; ignore pacing and packetisation.
findings.correction: A sender has MSS 1,460 bytes, cwnd = 40 segments, the receiver advertises rwnd = 256 KiB (262,144 bytes), and 30,000 bytes are currently unacknowledged. How many more bytes may it send right now? Use the simplified new-data budget, with consistent ACK/window origins, no recovery/probe exceptions, and sufficient queued data; ignore pacing and packetisation.
findings.reason: Correct binary unit notation.

findings.original: Above ssthresh, the sender is near the path's limit and probes gently: **cwnd grows by one MSS per RTT**.
findings.correction: In classic Reno congestion avoidance, the sender probes with approximately **one MSS of cwnd growth per RTT** under ideal ACK/traffic assumptions. Crossing ssthresh does not prove that the path is currently near capacity.
findings.reason: The threshold is algorithm state, not an observation of current spare capacity.

findings.original: Sustaining full rate would need a loss rate below about one in five billion packets
findings.correction: In the distinct average-window model in RFC 3649, sustaining this average rate requires roughly one congestion event per five billion packets
findings.reason: Separate average-window model from peak-window recovery calculation.

findings.original: Pacing gain about 2.89; doubles like slow start until the delivery rate stops growing
findings.correction: Pacing gain about 2.89, designed for rapid growth; exits after three qualifying rounds without 25% bandwidth growth
findings.reason: Exact BBRv1 pipe-full test is less than25% growth across3 eligible rounds, not zero growth.

findings.original: the sender keeps in flight at most min(cwnd, rwnd), so rate ≈ cwnd / RTT.
findings.correction: both windows constrain ordinary new-data sending. A continuously backlogged, cwnd-limited steady flow has rate ≈ cwnd / RTT.
findings.reason: Window reductions cannot instantaneously remove flight; rate approximation needs stated limiting assumptions.

findings.original: Reno's linear growth can't fill fast, long paths; CUBIC grows as a cubic function of time since the last loss and backs off by 30%.
findings.correction: Reno’s linear growth can recover very slowly on high-BDP paths. CUBIC uses a time-based cubic target, a Reno-friendly region and normally a 30% congestion-event reduction.
findings.reason: Avoid absolute impossibility and distinguish cubic target from actual ACK-driven evolution.

findings.original: That's how long slow start would take to double from 1 to ~65,000 segments (about 17 RTTs). But after duplicate ACKs Reno is in congestion avoidance, growing linearly.
findings.correction: That's how long slow start would take to grow from 1 to at least 83,333 segments (17 ideal doubling rounds). But after duplicate ACKs Reno is in congestion avoidance, growing linearly.
findings.reason: 2^16=65536 while17doublings=131072; align arithmetic with target.

findings.original: That would limit the call's own throughput, not make pings to everywhere slow. The shared uplink queue affects all traffic.
findings.correction: A small receive window can limit that connection’s sending allowance, but it does not by itself explain the observed load-correlated ping delay. A shared uplink queue is the leading hypothesis; queue classes and traffic paths determine which packets are affected.
findings.reason: Remove universal all-traffic queue impact and unsupported pings-to-everywhere statement.

findings.original: That's how QUIC behaves, because it knows about streams. TCP has a single sequence space.
findings.correction: QUIC removes the requirement for a stream to wait solely for another stream’s missing bytes. Shared flow control, congestion control and application dependencies can still delay delivery. TCP uses one ordered byte stream.
findings.reason: Immediate QUIC delivery is not guaranteed.

findings.original: Browsers don't react to individual losses like this; the data is already on its way on the existing connection.
findings.correction: TCP handles this gap on the existing connection. The supplied scenario does not imply that the browser opens a replacement connection; doing so would require application-level recovery logic.
findings.reason: Avoid universal browser behavior claim.

findings.original:
Mathis: `rate ∝ 1 / (RTT × √p)`.

1. RTT: 20 → 80 ms, a factor of 4. Rate ÷ 4.
2. Loss: 0.01% → 0.04%, a factor of 4. √4 = 2, so rate ÷ 2.
3. Combined: ÷ 8.

```
71.2 / 8 = ~8.9 Mbit/s
```

Distance and loss compound. This is a core reason CDNs put servers near users.
findings.correction:
Mathis: `rate ∝ 1 / (RTT × √p)`.

1. RTT: 20 → 80 ms, a factor of 4. Rate ÷ 4.
2. Loss: 0.01% → 0.04%, a factor of 4. √4 = 2, so rate ÷ 2.
3. Combined: ÷ 8.

```
71.2 / 8 = ~8.9 Mbit/s
```

The model’s RTT and loss factors compound. Closer servers can reduce propagation delay, but geographic distance alone does not determine RTT or measured throughput.
findings.reason: Do not equate RTT with distance.

findings.original: Correct. In B, the minimum delay over every 100 ms interval stays above 5 ms, which signals a standing queue. The senders' congestion control then shrinks their windows.
findings.correction: Correct. In B, the minimum delay over every 100 ms interval stays above 5 ms, which signals a standing queue. Responsive senders can reduce their offered load; the response depends on the protocol, controller and delivered feedback.
findings.reason: AQM does not force every sender to use a window or respond.

findings.original: TCP has up to 40 bytes of options. The problem is that the network interferes with new ones, not that there's no space.
findings.correction: The base TCP header allows up to 40 option bytes. That finite space can constrain extensions too, but it is not zero; unfamiliar-option handling by middleboxes is a separate deployment obstacle.
findings.reason: Option space is limited and can itself be an obstacle.

findings.original: The checksum covers each segment and is computed by the kernel, independent of application messages.
findings.correction: TCP checksums cover segments, independently of application message framing. They may be computed by the protocol stack or hardware offload; a kernel implementation is not required.
findings.reason: Avoid claiming all TCP checksums computed in kernel.

findings.original: Ephemeral ports are used for outgoing connections. A server binding a fixed port isn't affected.
findings.correction: Exhaustion of automatically selected local ports is a different failure mode. Here the supplied diagnostics identify retained TIME_WAIT state affecting an explicit bind; an existing conflicting allocation can also matter when a chosen fixed port overlaps the automatic range.
findings.reason: Fixed-port listeners can be affected by actual ephemeral allocations; diagnose supplied scenario.

findings.original: Threads can call recv(), and blocking I/O releases the GIL. 50,000 processes would be even heavier than 50,000 threads.
findings.correction: Threads can call recv(); in CPython’s usual GIL-enabled build, blocking socket I/O releases the GIL. Replacing each native thread with a process adds separate process-management costs and does not remove the need to measure resource limits.
findings.reason: Version/runtime scope and remove unmeasured categorical capacity comparison.

findings.original: The peer is still connected; it just isn't reading. There's no broken pipe, only a growing backlog.
findings.correction: Not reading replies does not itself require an immediate BrokenPipeError. Queued output can grow while the connection remains usable; independent failures or later endpoint closure are still possible.
findings.reason: Absence of reader does not prove no concurrent error.
